The Laughing dove (Spilopelia senegalensis) is a widespread Afro-Asian columbid whose reproductive and developmental parameters show considerable plasticity under different thermal regimes. For eggs incubated at a temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], the incubation period yields an age at birth of 12.5 days [ab = 12.5 days], a duration that reflects the typical altricial development pattern of small doves. Nestlings emerge weighing an initial wet weight of 6.6 grams [Ww0 = 6.6 grams], a modest mass at hatching that requires intensive parental provisioning through the early nestling phase. As development proceeds under the warmer conditions typical of the active season, often around 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], the fledging stage is reached at 15.5 days after hatching [tx = 15.5 days after hatching], at which point the young are capable of short flights but remain dependent on adults for several additional weeks.

At a stable ambient temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], the developmental trajectory of Laughing doves continues with the attainment of sexual maturity, which occurs at 46 days after hatching [tp = 46 days after hatching]. This relatively early puberty allows individuals to integrate into the breeding population within their first season, though the onset of gonadal activity does not immediately translate into reproductive output. The first successful brood is not initiated until 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], a delay that likely reflects the time required for territory establishment, pair bonding, and the accumulation of sufficient body condition at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This interval is consistent with the life-history strategy of many small columbids, which prioritize survival and condition over precocious breeding despite early physiological maturation.

The species exhibits a modest maximum reproductive rate, constrained by its typical clutch of a single egg per nesting attempt [N_R_i = single egg per nesting attempt] and a clutch frequency of one brood per year [F_R_i = one brood per year], both measured under conditions of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This low annual output is characteristic of tropical and subtropical Columbidae, where extended parental care and high adult survival compensate for low fecundity. The rate is also reflected in the population's slow turnover, as the relatively high energy demands of chick rearing limit the number of successful breeding cycles annually. Comparative data from related species suggest that this reproductive strategy is linked to stable, resource-predictable environments where competition for nesting sites can be intense, favoring investment in individual offspring quality over brood quantity.

Adult body mass in Laughing doves shows pronounced sexual dimorphism, with the ultimate wet weight for females reaching 98.4 grams [Wwi = 98.4 grams] while males attain a larger ultimate wet weight of 104.4 grams [Wwi = 104.4 grams]. This size disparity is common among columbids and may be related to male territorial defense and courtship displays, which favor larger body size. In contrast, the initial wet weight at hatching is only 5 grams [Wwb = 5 grams], a value that underscores the altricial state of the neonate and its dependence on parental thermoregulation and feeding. The substantial increase from this hatching mass to adult dimensions requires a prolonged period of growth and high metabolic expenditure, supported by the crop-milk production characteristic of the family.

Under controlled conditions at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], Laughing doves have been documented to reach a maximum age of approximately 13.3 years [am = approximately 13.3 years]. This longevity is notable for a bird of this body size and aligns with the generally extended lifespans observed in columbids, which are attributed to their low extrinsic mortality in benign habitats and their efficient metabolic economy. The basal metabolic rate, measured as 152.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 152.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a thermoneutral temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], reflects the energetic cost of maintaining this slow pace of life. Together, the modest reproductive output, relatively high adult survival, and substantial longevity paint a picture of a species adapted to stable, warm climates where long-term persistence is favored over rapid population turnover.
